crestedfireback.title: Bornean Crested Fireback — Jewel of the Lowland Forest
crestedfireback.description: The male Bornean Crested Fireback is a striking bird, with glossy blue-black plumage, a fiery chestnut back and a bare red face, strutting through the forest floor with a confident, prancing step. It depends on intact lowland rainforest, exactly the habitat being lost fastest in Borneo to logging and palm oil expansion. Shy and ground-dwelling, it is hard to observe, and sightings usually come in the quiet early morning. Its population is declining as forests fragment, which is why it is considered Vulnerable. Protecting lowland forest corridors is the single most important step in keeping this beautiful pheasant alive.

egyptianvulture.title: Egyptian Vulture — The Clever Scavenger
egyptianvulture.location: Across Africa, Southern Europe & South Asia
egyptianvulture.description: Easily recognised by its pale cream plumage and yellow face, the Egyptian Vulture is one of the few birds known to use tools, picking up stones to crack open ostrich eggs. It is also a long-distance migrant, with many European birds wintering in Africa and India. Despite its intelligence, the species has declined sharply from poisoning, collisions with power lines, and veterinary drugs that contaminate carcasses. Vultures are nature's clean-up crew, preventing disease by disposing of dead animals quickly. Losing them has real consequences for ecosystems and for people, which makes the recovery of this species an urgent priority.

hawkeagle.title: Changeable Hawk-Eagle — Master of the Forest Edge
hawkeagle.description: The Changeable Hawk-Eagle earns its name from its many colour forms, with crested and non-crested individuals and a wide range of plumage tones. It hunts from a concealed perch in the forest canopy, launching in a swift, powerful dash after birds, squirrels and lizards. In flight, its broad rounded wings and long tail give it great agility among trees. Though not currently threatened globally, it relies on healthy woodland, and local populations suffer when forests are cleared. Keeping an eye on the status of common species like this one is how conservation catches problems early.

indianvulture.title: Indian Vulture — A Collapse and a Comeback Attempt
indianvulture.description: In the 1990s the Indian Vulture was among the most abundant large birds of prey in the world. Within a few years, populations crashed by more than ninety-five percent, and the cause was traced to diclofenac, a veterinary painkiller that was lethal to vultures feeding on treated cattle. The drug has since been banned for veterinary use in India, and captive breeding programmes now hold birds for eventual release. Recovery is slow, because vultures breed only once a year and raise a single chick. This species is a powerful lesson in how quickly an unseen threat can collapse a seemingly secure population.

maleo.title: Maleo — The Bird That Buries Its Eggs
maleo.description: The Maleo is a striking, chicken-sized bird found only on the island of Sulawesi, and its breeding habits are extraordinary. Rather than incubating eggs, it buries them in warm volcanic or sun-heated sand and leaves them to hatch alone. The chicks emerge fully developed and ready to fly within hours. This strategy depends on a small number of traditional nesting grounds, which are threatened by egg collection, habitat loss and disturbance. Community-led protection programmes, where villagers help relocate and guard eggs, have offered hope. The Maleo shows how closely a species' survival can be tied to a few special places.

whiterumpedvulture.title: White-rumped Vulture — Guardian of the Skies
whiterumpedvulture.description: Once among the most numerous raptors on the planet, the White-rumped Vulture suffered the same collapse as its Indian relatives, losing the overwhelming majority of its population within a decade. Its distinctive white lower back is visible when the bird soars in thermals above villages and fields. Beyond diclofenac poisoning, it faces loss of nesting trees and shortage of safe food. Dedicated vulture safe zones, where poisonous drugs are controlled, are now helping a slow stabilisation in some regions. Seeing one overhead today is both a joy and a reminder that recovery is possible only with sustained effort.
